summary: Reports a working system at Xerox in Palo Alto for sending text display information between a DEC PDP-10 running TENEX and a remote IMLAC PDS-1 display. It covers the IMLAC hardware, the facilities the user sees and the monitor calls on the TENEX side.

eli5.summary: A big computer sends words to a little screen far away. This note explains how the screen and the computer talk.

questions: how did the pdp-10 communicate with an imlac display
what was the tenex imlac system
subtitle: Connecting a main computer to remote graphics displays through text messages.

tldr.problem: Engineers need a way to send display information from a powerful main computer to remote graphical display terminals for interactive applications.
tldr.mechanism: The system divides responsibilities: the main PDP-10 validates commands and allocates display resources, while the remote IMLAC display processes messages and renders text and graphics.
tldr.outcome: Users could interact with a single display split into multiple areas, switching between graphical and text modes without losing information.

today: RFC 190 describes a working system from July 1971. It represents an early implementation of networked graphical displays and illustrates the design trade-offs of splitting display logic between a central computer and a remote terminal.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 190 describes an operational system built at Xerox Palo Alto Research Center for sending display information from a DEC PDP-10 with TENEX (the main computer) to a remote IMLAC PDS-1 (a graphics display terminal). The system lets programs send text and graphics commands over a serial connection, enabling interactive display applications across a network or long distance.
sections.eli5: One computer can control a screen far away by giving it directions, just like texting instructions to someone drawing on a board.

sections.title: The IMLAC Hardware and Display Modes
sections.content: The IMLAC is a 16-bit minicomputer with 4K words of core memory, a cycle-stealing display, a keyboard, and an asynchronous serial interface. The display can draw characters using very short vectors, and optionally supports long vectors. The system offers two display modes: display mode shows text strings at arbitrary positions on the screen allocated to users in rectangular display areas, and teletype simulation mode shows the last 20 to 30 lines of text output like a teletype. Each display has a cursor that follows a pointing device (typically a mouse), and programs can switch between modes without losing content.
sections.eli5: The screen is like a notepad: you can write words anywhere on it, or switch to show line-by-line like an old typewriter, and a cursor follows your mouse.

sections.title: System Calls and Message Formats
sections.content: The PDP-10 controls the IMLAC through JSYS monitor calls. Key calls include ADA (assign a display area with coordinates and default text properties), STRDA (write, move, or delete a string within a display area), and SCSR (set the cursor string). The system uses an escape character (code 33 octal) to mark command sequences in the message stream. Commands are prefixed with a character count and contain encoded parameters such as display area identifiers (using 12 bits split across two characters), string identifiers, font specifications, and X-Y coordinates. The PDP-10 validates all commands, checking display area identifiers and string numbers, so the IMLAC does not need to send responses for each command.
sections.eli5: The computer sends short codes: one says 'put a box here', another says 'write this word in that box', another says 'move the word'. The screen figures out what to show.

sections.title: How the Two Machines Divide Work
sections.content: The design allocates validity checking to the PDP-10: it allocates and validates display area identifiers and string numbers, making the IMLAC mostly stateless. Display areas are numbered system-wide, while string identifiers are numbered from 1 to N within each display area. The only errors the PDP-10 cannot detect are transmission parity errors and IMLAC memory overflow. A secondary design goal was to minimize the number of characters needed to represent each display command, using multi-bit fields and character counts to pack information efficiently.
sections.eli5: The big computer does all the thinking about what is allowed; the screen just draws. This keeps the screen program simple.
